utterances.text: Teeth have the priority, if they're present. If they're not, then the next option is the femur.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In relation to this autopsy, you told us that you carried -- that you took DNA samples before the bodies were examined and that that was not the usual procedure. Why didn't you follow the normal procedure on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: For a certain reason. People who decided on the procedure asked that the DNA sample be taken first. I am usually against that, because you never know, before having examined every single body, whether there is a surplus body. On that day, representatives of the two commissions turned up. A doctor came from Banja Luka. The crime technicians were there. And I believe and I dare say the things on that day were done ad hoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, you've said that in general, photographs are taken of the bodies during an autopsy. Do you know, were photographs taken that day of these remains?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: On that day, when we were taking the samples, photos were taken. On my part, I could only insist on observing the taking of the photographs and that every bone sample be placed in a bag and that it be marked with a "KT" marking of the prosecution, the prosecution and the number of the body, and then every bag would be sealed. At the end, a photo of all the taken samples was taken as one photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, after the samples were taken, you told us that you examined, washed and reconstructed the bodies; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: That's the procedure. First the bones are washed, then the body is reconstructed, and then the autopsy begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And do you know, were photographs taken of the reconstructed bodies?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: I know once I finished the procedure, I called the inspector and the crime technicians in this case from the cantonal MUP. I usually make a note of the time that the photos are taken, so I'm sure that I will be able to find that in my report, the date and the time. On 10 July 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you have copies of those photographs, if any, with you?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: I never keep any photos. This is part of the photo documentation that is kept either by the prosecutor or by the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, the DNA samples, you've told us, were sent off to the ICMP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: Samples are not sent off to the ICMP -- oh, no, I'm sorry, you're right. I apologise. Yes, the ICMP, yes, that's the international commission, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like to clarify something in your statement. At paragraph 22 of the statement, you said that the ICMP sent their original findings back to you. What is meant by "original findings"?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: I believe that this should have been the other way around. I thought that those were preliminary findings, because the bodies had not been processed, and the ICMP sends me their findings after the matching between the bones and the blood, and this is the only form of findings I ever received from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So the findings that ICMP send to you, those are preliminary findings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: No. In our cases -- actually, it says here a possible identity. This is the final findings. After that, we don't receive anything else. There's no further confirmation. This is the final findings from the laboratory and narrowing down the identification to 99.9 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'll come back to this topic a little bit later. What I'd just like to check with you is -- yes, it's something that you said in response to the Prosecution -- the Prosecutor. You were shown one of the DNA reports, and you said that as soon as the first finding arrived, "the bodies no longer stayed with me." Can you just explain that in a bit more detail, please, what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: As soon as the initial findings arrived from the ICMP with the names of the persons of Serbian ethnicity, the hand-over of the bodies was carried out. I am not sure. It may be that the findings kept on coming, but they came to the doctor in Banja Luka. The bodies were no longer in Visoko by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: From your evidence, I had the impression that the normal practice would be for you to hold on to the bodies after the initial findings arrived. Would that have been so that you could have carried out further investigation?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: These bodies were not finished, from the medical point of view, I would say. We have an example here of DNA findings, Kamenica 177, where the skull belonged to the body. We also have part of the body 1/7A, of Bozidar Todorovic, which continues. The body -- we have a bone here, but under -- an elbow bone. But now under 144 [as interpreted] we have the same person appearing, Bozidar Todorovic, with a femoral bone, which means that one part of the body was on the number 114 and the other part of the body was under 117. If you look at my findings -- let me not complicate the matter, and let me try and put it in simple terms. What you can find at the body 1/7, for example, is missing with the body of 1/4, and it is possible that both bones belong to one and the same person. In practical terms, we have a femoral bone, we have an elbow bone in two different places, under two different numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Let's try to clarify that. You mentioned a few things there. So initial findings came in from ICMP. In your view, the bodies were not finished with, from the medical point of view. However, you had to send the bodies away before you could complete a proper and thorough investigation; is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: Correct. Neither medical procedure nor the identification were complete. The DNA findings is merely one segment of the whole identification process.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you know why the bodies were sent away before the -- before a full investigation could be completed?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: I really -- believe me, I did not go into those reasons. I just do my bit, the bit that is the doctor's part. Unfortunately, some people interfere with that and then they prevent you from completing your part of the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Right. I'd like to ask you about the report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying, Doctor, that you didn't complete the job finally? In other words, the bodies were never brought back to you to complete your job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bodies were not returned to me, and the job was not finished because that person did not end up having all of their bones and they were not ready for identification, although it was possible for the colleague in Banja Luka to continue working where I left it off, using my findings and the DNA results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you just answer my question with a "yes" or a "no"? You never finally completed the job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to know. I didn't understand. You may proceed, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And just to clarify, you said that people interfered, and you've told us that the remains were sent to Banja Luka. Could you tell us, who interfered in this process?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: The first person who issues order and whose orders I have to carry out is the cantonal prosecutor. If the prosecutor decides to hand the bodies over to a different doctor, in agreement with the Commission, it is not up to me to change that decision. I am not even in a position to do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So it's the prosecutor who decided that the bodies have to be sent off to Banja Luka before the investigation could be completed?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: Since I swore to be telling the truth at the beginning of my testimony, I have to say that this is the ugly part that I never really investigated. I just took the papers, the record of the hand-over, which says that the hand-over had been agreed. Sometimes the situation is the other way around. For example, we had bodies in Banja Luka that had been identified as Muslims, and those bodies, after the procedure, were delivered to us and were available to us for subsequent examination or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So just to clarify the question, was it the prosecutor that decided that the bodies had to go to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: I can only assume he was the person responsible for the bodies, because he followed the bodies from the beginning of the exhumation, and I believe that nobody's in a position to do anything without the prosecutor's express approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And when you say the bodies were sent to Banja Luka, by that, they were sent to the appropriate authorities in Republika Srpska; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I found the paper that I have. It was signed by the cantonal prosecutor, and it says the subject is the hand-over of the bodily remains, where he explains. I happen to have that because I prepared for this trial. Otherwise, this isn't my line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Could you just tell us, please, what the prosecutor orders in that document?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: He's not ordering here. It says that the subject -- under "Subject," it is the hand-over of the bodily remains. It says: "Document 0146405, 2006, of the 13th of September 2006, the Federal Commission for Missing Persons of Sarajevo went to the prosecutor with the request to hand over the remains of the persons exhumed in Kamenica Municipality in order to hand over --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A little slower, please, could the witness read slower?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you read slower, please, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where did I get to? Where were you able to follow me? Up to what point?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. " ... Kamenica Municipality in order to hand over ...," and then you disappeared from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The locality of Kamenica, Zavidovici Municipality, in order to hand over the latter to the Office for Missing and Captured Persons of Republika Srpska, with the aim of establishing the final identification process. In this connection, the Federal Commission for Missing Persons is given permission to take all the bodily remains of the bodies exhumed at the Kamenica locality of Zavidovici Municipality, in the case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe this is an exhibit, and it might be just easier to show the witness the exhibit again, because I believe this came in through the previous witness, yes, the hand-over --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not in a position to confirm that. It's -- without knowing the date or any of the details, I can't say. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But is there a document? I mean, this witness here is not a fact witness, she's an expert witness, and I think you are trying to test her memory on anything. If there's a document we can show her, if she can tell us and it will cut down a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Sure. Your Honour, I don't have that exhibit at hand, so I cannot confirm from what we just heard whether or not the exhibit is that same document. But perhaps what I could just simply ask to the witness and move on is this:

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, Doctor, from that document it's clear that the body remains are to be sent onwards to the Office for Missing and Captured Persons of Republika Srpska for final identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In other words, final identification was still to take place at the time that that document was issued?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, is that what the witness said?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What line? Oh, yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's just disappeared. Fifty-four, line 7 or 8, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've seen it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that, I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So would you agree with me, Doctor, that according to that document, final identification is to take place once the remains had been sent on to the Office for Missing and Captured Persons for Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: Judging by this document that I just read out together with you, it means that they were sent on for final identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Doctor, I'd like to turn to your report. You have a hard copy in front of you there; is that right? Just so I'm not repeating myself in respect of each body, can you confirm that all of the bodies that you mention in your report were in a skeletalised condition?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: That's what it says in all the findings. As no tissues are found, osteological examination is conducted of the skeleton, which means the skeletons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to turn to 1/1, the first body. Perhaps, please, if this -- if the expert report could be brought up on our screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 654.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And I believe it's going to be page number 3 in the English version. I can refer to the Bosnian page number, if necessary, unless the doctor has her report in front of her. If you'll just bear with me a moment. So 1/1 starts at the page before this in English, so if we can just go back one page, please. It's the next page in B/C/S. If we go to the bottom of that page in the English version, please. So here we can see where findings 1/1 begins. If we can go on to the next page, please, and see the doctor's findings. And if we can scroll towards -- this is fine. If we can go down -- go down, please. And perhaps if we can just enlarge the page so we can see the -- that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, Doctor, in respect of these body remains, we can see that the head was missing and also the bones of the hands and feet were missing; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: As it says here, the body was incomplete. And then I state what was missing on that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Go on to the next page in English, in the English version, please. If we can go to the top of the page, we can see, Doctor, that there was a cut to the sixth cervical vertebrae and also linear fractures to both shoulder blades. A little bit further down, we can see your conclusion, and what you say is: "The changes found in the part of the above-described cervical vertebrae point to an action of a broadly-swung blade belonging to a hard mechanical object." You then go on to conclude: "The death was probably violent and arrived as a result of a complete interruption of the continuity of the cervical spine, which also resulted in the separation of the head from the body." Now, I have a few questions for you about this. First of all, you've confirmed that this was a skeletonised body and that there were bones missing from the hands and the feet and also the skull. This Trial Chamber has heard evidence, and, Your Honours, I can give you the reference if necessary, in which a witness was asked the following question: "Is it your assessment that the bodies that were found at the Kamenica grave were initially buried at some other location and then subsequently dug up and moved to the Kamenica location?" That witness answered: "Yes." He was then asked: "So this would mean that the burial location at Kamenica was a secondary burial location?" And to that the witness said: "Yes." Now, based on what you saw of the findings -- sorry, what you saw of the body remains, would you agree with what that witness had to say, that there was evidence here that these body remains had been moved at some stage?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: Since most of the bodies were incomplete, and not only the tissue was missing, but the bones, too, then in fact it was a case of bodies that had been transferred, but probably in the skeletal state for such small bone fragments to have been lost. The bodies moved, because bodies, if they're not moved, then they're found in continuity, as we say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: All right. So you say in fact it was a case of bodies that had been transferred. If the bodies had been transferred, it would follow from that that at some earlier stage, the bodies would have to have been dug up from another location; would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. And now I just wanted to emphasise one point, and this is where it's important that I wasn't on location, because you can see a lot if you're on site. You can see the position of the bodies and make your deductions. So if there were photographs taken, you could also see that on the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So if the bodies had been removed from a primary burial location to the Kamenica grave which was a secondary burial location, it would be logical to assume that some sort of tools or equipment had been used to move those bodies; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: It depends if the bodies are on the surface or if they're dug deep into the ground. I'm not an expert in that area, so I can't really say. But from my aspect, from my own aspect, I can say that there were no technical injuries, major technical injuries on the body, which you can see if there is rough manipulation of the bodies, the bodies are roughly handled.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I know that we're speculating to a certain extent, but if the bodies had been buried at the primary location and they had been dug out of the ground, it's possible, is it not, that the bodies could have been damaged during the process of removing them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Has the witness not said it depends on whether the bodies were dug up from under the ground or were on the surface of the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Doctor, you said that there were no technical injuries, major technical injuries, but you would agree with me they were --

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: On the basis of my experience, I say that if you have the skeletal remains, then you can see if an excavator has been used, or picks and shovels. They're the kind of rough marks that you could notice on skeletal remains. But if they were carefully transported, that's different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Doctor, returning back to body 1/1, in your report you note that there are linear fractures of both shoulder blades. Now, you agree that the bodies were transferred to the Kamenica gravesite. Would you accept that it's possible that the shoulder blades were damaged during the process of transfer?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: These bones, especially in part of the body, are sometimes damaged through pressure of the earth on them. Some bones are susceptible to changes in the atmosphere where they're dug in. And we very often find fractures of this type in bodies that have not been moved and transferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So those are some of the possible causes of the fractures, but is also another possible cause the process of movement, transfer from one location to another?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: Possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the damage to the cervical vertebrae, you say that that points to the action of a hard mechanical object. If it was the case that these bodies were dug from the ground at the primary burial location, would you agree with me that it is possible that the equipment used to dig out the bodies could constitute the hard mechanical object which caused the damage to this vertebrae?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: I've already said, and it also says in my findings, that there is a clear distinction between damages where fractures are stipulated and where the cut surfaces are stated. So the vertebrae has a small surface area, and of the means used at exhumations, it is rare that damages of this kind are caused. This is an injury, not a damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Am I right in saying you don't have any photographs or anything with you in which you could demonstrate to us what you've just explained?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: I don't have any photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I want to go back to what you've just said in your testimony shortly before you concluded your examination-in-chief. The Prosecutor asked you about establishing cause of death, and what you said is: "The exact cause of death cannot be established." And you mentioned that a lot of time went by, and you can't say whether the -- and this is in relation to the damage to the vertebrae, you can't say whether that was caused during life or immediately after death. You recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you to the conclusion that you've put in this report in relation to 1/1. And what you said was: "The death was probably violent and arrived as a result of a complete interruption of the continuity of the cervical spine, which resulted in a separation of the head from the body." You can't say whether the vertebrae or the spine was severed while the person was alive or after they were dead, can you?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: That's what I said, that at this point in time you can no longer establish whether this injury was caused during the person's life or after the person had died.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Then may I ask you, why did you put this conclusion in your report, that death was probably violent and arrived as a result of a complete interruption? If you didn't know that for certain, why did you speculate and include that in the report?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: It is our practice that when stating our opinion, we can stipulate what changes or injuries on the body we consider to be the possible cause of death. And I've already said that we're dealing with injuries which, when found on a skeleton, are incompatible with life, and that would be injuries to the vertebrae, because we have politrauma, as I've said, where other bones were fractured as well, the long bones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that what you've concluded here is rather stronger than what you consider to be the possible cause of death? You have stated that death arrived "as a result." In other words, as I understand your report, you are saying with certainty that that was the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In fairness to the witness, Mr. Robson, if you read that sentence from its beginning, it says that the "the death was probably," and if you accept that probability, then the part that you are reading would become true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take on board what you're saying, but essentially it may be a language matter, but what I'm trying to explore is: Does the "probably" just attach to the "violent" or does the "probably" attach to the violent part and the latter conclusion, and that's what I'm trying to explore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but the sentence clearly says: "If you accept the probability that death was a result of violence, which resulted in that interruption," then of course you would come to the conclusion that that violence is the one that caused the separation of the head from the body, only if you accept the probability.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my submission, it's open to interpretation, and I'm trying to explore what the witness was trying to state here. So, Doctor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But, you see, my concern is when you say her conclusion is firm and strong, but it is based on the probability. It's only firm to the extent that the probability is found to be true.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain. May I be allowed to explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may do so, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I write my findings, and every grave has its specific features, then usually I conduct an analysis of the bodies and then I form an opinion, and I put in the probability element. Now, following these bodies and the injuries found on them, if on, for example, body number 1 you have an injury to the fourth cervical vertebra and then on body 2 you don't have the first and second vertebrae, and then on body 4 you have an injury to the third cervical vertebra, and on body 5, for example, you also have an injury to the third cervical vertebra, then on body 7 you have the same injury of the third and fourth cervical vertebrae, then that indicates a probability, a greater probability of those being injuries than damages -- rather than damages, injuries rather than damages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Doctor. What I was trying to explore with you, and please correct me if my understanding is incorrect, but in your conclusion for body 1/1, are you saying that death arrived as a result, in other words, it was definite that death arrived as a result of the vertebrae being interrupted, or are you just saying that that was a possibility?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: First of all, in my finding, you don't have a conclusion anywhere. There's no section entitled "Conclusion," with a conclusion. So you can look at this as an autopsy or an examination. After an autopsy and the examination, you come to the expertise, expert finding, and only then do all the other circumstances in the case come into play. And then within the frameworks of all that, when you have all the facts and circumstances, can you say with greater certain -- can you discuss this with greater certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Right. So if I understand you correctly, this deals -- this report deals with the autopsy, but it doesn't deal with the expert finding which would have occurred had a further examination of the bodies taken place?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: No. In my line of work, you have your first step, and that is the examination, that's the first step, or the autopsy if the body is complete. Those are the first steps. And then all the injuries and changes that you come across are recorded for an opinion to be established on the basis of the changes. Now, in my country, the process is as follows: Then you go on to an expert examination where you have insight into all the different components, and when the Court or some other institution establishes certain facts and then comes back to me and asks me, "Is that how that could have happened," when they have something concrete-specific to look at, then we take another look and see whether what I have and the other circumstances of the case match, whether they are -- whether they are in keeping with one another. So this is not a definite opinion in the sense of cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So no expert findings have been carried out in relation to these remains; this report we have relates to the earlier stage alone?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: The first step.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Right. I'll move on and try and move quickly through the other remains. If we could turn to I think it's page number 4 in the English version, a document. It's body -- the body remains 1/2. It's probably the next -- if we can turn to the next page, please. If we could go to the page after that as well, please. And if we can scroll down to the bottom. So, Doctor, in this report you discuss the parts of the body which are missing from these body remains. With this body, the head is missing, but it's right, isn't it, that there's nothing to suggest, in relation to this body, that the head was severed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If the head is missing, how was it not severed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in respect of -- well, let me explore that with the witness and I'll try to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Doctor, in relation to the other body remains where you have stated that there's a possibility that the head has been -- the spine has been interrupted, in relation to this body, there's no markings on the cervical vertebrae to suggest that the vertebrae have been cut at any time; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: As can be seen in the findings, no, there isn't a description of that, so there were no injuries, except to say that the first and second and seventh cervical vertebrae were missing. And in this part of the findings, you might have noticed that there is no opinion as to the probable cause of death, no opinion is stated, because if you apply the same analogy with this body, you have the linear fracture of the left shoulder blade, which I said was frequent under the impact of the weight of the earth, or the small damages, so I don't state the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So in relation to these body remains, is it possible that the skull could have become detached from the body by the natural process of deterioration, and when the body remains were moved, the skull was perhaps left behind?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: That is always possible, if the body is in the stage of skeletalisation. Mostly, the head will become separated from the rest of the body, if we are talking about a skeleton.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Moving on to body remains 1/3, if we could please move on to the next page in the document on our screens. And if we can go to the next page again in the English version. In respect of these remains, Doctor, you've noted that there were cuts in the shin-bones of the skeleton. Do you see that in your report?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: You mean on page 3 or page 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I think it's page 5 in your document, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: On page 5, I can see body number 1/4. Are we talking about that body or the body 1/3?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's probably the page before. You describe the condition of the body and you note that there are cuts in both the left shinbone and also the right shinbone. Do you recall making those findings in relation to this body?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: I remember, and I have it in my findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this is evidence that could suggest that the bodies were damaged by tools during the process of either digging them out of the ground or moving them to this secondary burial location?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: I repeat and I emphasise, the tools used for digging are, for the most part, a shovel or similar things. Here we can see cuts with a very short space between these cuts. They run parallel to each other. Usually when digging out the bodies, when one encounters a body, and bear in mind that these bodies are in a good state to this day, so usually when you encounter a body, you can feel that and you can hear the sound of the tool hitting that bone. That is why my opinion is that these cuts were not the result of damage incurred during the digging out of the body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, could we elicit from the witness some sort of knowledge about how soon does a body become a skeleton, how many years after its burial?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Doctor, could you help us with that? I would imagine the answer is, "It depends," but if you could please assist with that question.

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: The answer will be: It depends. It depends on the conditions. I had bodies in which skeletalisation started after 11 days, or actually 11 days after the burial, there was nothing but a skeleton. But we also come across bodies or skeletons that are covered with tissue, they are mummified but they do have tissue. It all depends on the conditions of the soil in which the body is buried, especially bearing in mind that a majority of these bodies -- and I don't know about these particular ones, but a majority of these bodies were wrapped either in clothes or in some sort of sacks, so the tissue must have been preserved for longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So just to go back, you mentioned that the cuts you saw in the shin-bones were parallel cuts. That could be some sort of tool, couldn't it, as opposed to a weapon?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: I will again quote an example and tell you that in the same way as in the vertebrae, and in the same way as in the body number 3, number 4, the cuts are on both shin-bones and they are very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: But, again, you don't exclude the possibility that it was some sort of tool that caused these markings?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: There may be a tool that I've not seen or heard of before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: All right. I want to move to 1/6. If we could please move through the report. We can move forward about four or five -- four pages. It's the seventh page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now Doctor, in respect of these body remains, you have given your opinion that the extremities of the long bones, collarbones and ribs show that damage occurred after death. Do you see that in your statement? It's in the next page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, on page 7, you mean? I said the extremities of the long bones, the collarbones and ribs, with damage inflicted postmortem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: There is even a part where I found the damage of the fracture edges, which was inflicted postmortem. In other words, every fracture edge is observed in order to see whether any subsequent damage was inflicted to the fracture edge postmortem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And I think you said earlier in your evidence that there was a lot of damage to this particular body. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I said, about this body, that it had suffered a politrauma, that there were fractures in addition to the evident damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And can you confirm for us, from looking at your report, that again there's no evidence which indicates that any of the cervical vertebrae had been cut on this particular body?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: First and second, first and second. Go to the beginning under anthropological analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Doctor, the first and second vertebrae were missing, but rather like the earlier body, there's no evidence to show that there were any cuts to any of the other cervical vertebrae?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: This is not mentioned in the findings. It is also -- it is only said that these vertebrae are missing. And further on in the findings, it is not stated that they were found on the other vertebrae.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can just turn over the page to the second-from-last sentence in relation to this body.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Body number 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, body number 6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Doctor, what you say there is that the death was probably violent as a result of a politrauma. Does this conflict with what you say earlier, where you've described that the damage, in your opinion, occurred after death? So earlier, in relation to this body, you discuss how damage was caused after death, in your opinion, and yet you've concluded that the death was probably violent as a result of a politrauma. Is it possible to explain that?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. You are only pointing to the first part of the description, where the damage is described. However, below that you will see "a spiral fracture of the right clavicle." A spiral fracture does not result from damage. It rather occurs through torsion of an arm that offers resistance. As for the long bones, unlike the vertebrae, it is specific that they sometimes indicate that injuries were inflicted during the life of the person, because the outer layer of the bone tends to protect the bone during life. That is why the original, initial fracture is always accompanied with hairline fractures that are separate from the main or original fracture. Likewise --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Doctor, perhaps just to clarify this: Unlike the bodies where there was a cut to the cervical vertebrae, in relation to this body do you think there is a high likelihood that the death resulted from politrauma or, again, are you unable to say whether the politrauma occurred during life or after death?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: Based on the fractures on this body, which I mentioned and refer to them as "spiral fractures," and the depressed multi-fracture of the body of the right femur, I was able to state, in my opinion, that the death was probably violent and that it was the result of a politrauma.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, I want to move on to the last body remains we're going to discuss, 1/7. If at this stage I could please -- if the witness could please be shown a document. It's the DNA reports, which is Exhibit 649. If we could please look at page 2 in this document. Now, Doctor, you mentioned this person a little bit earlier, and I want to explore with you what you were discussing. We can see here a DNA report which bears the name "Bozidar Todoric." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: This is 1/4, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: That's correct. If we could move through the document to page 4 so we've -- again, this is another DNA report in respect of Bozidar Todoric, and we can see that here he bears -- the document bears the number "1/7". And then just as a -- to complete this, perhaps if we can turn to the next page in the document. Here we can see the third entry for the same named person, and this is number 1/7A. So according to the documents that we have here, the sample taken from remains 1/4 and 1/7 both match the same person. Could you explain how this has come about or how this may have come about?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: As I've already explained, for body number 1/7, these are samples taken from the body that was in a bag marked as "1/7". 1/7A is a sample of the elbow bone, i.e., one part of the body. Since this body had a skull, a head, a sample was also taken from a tooth in order to confirm that the head indeed belonged to the body. However, you can look at my findings and you will see that the body 1/7 is missing long bones of both legs, the long bones of both legs, and the femoral bone sample was sent off because the femoral bone was in the bag marked as "1/4". This speaks in the favour of the fact that the body had been removed from its original burial place, because the legs of that person was in the position 1/4 and the other part of the body was in position 1/7. This is an example of an unfinished business. This is where a body had to be completed for the business to be finished. Through an analysis of both bodies, at the face of it one might have concluded that all the bodies belonged to one person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So this is an unfinished --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. That last sentence, you're saying, "at the face of it one might have concluded that all the bodies belonged to one person." Did you mean to say something else, ma'am? One person can only have one body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Normally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Normally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In French, all body parts, not all the bodies. All body parts belonging to these bodies belong to one person, did they or not?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... rather than bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Something else was said in the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that the word "bodies" should be replaced by the word "bones."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter says we must replace the word "bodies" with "bones." Okay. Thank you. Mr. Robson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told by my colleague that the translation of the last part of the witness's -- oh, it's correct now, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, Doctor, you say that this is an example of unfinished business, this is where a body had to be completed for the business to be finished. By that, do you mean that you didn't have the opportunity to complete the full and proper investigation of these bodies?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll object at this point. I think this has been asked and answered several times, what she means by that. The process, I think it's been asked at least twice here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was a question of clarification, because I was trying to find out exactly what the witness meant by that response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But this witness is explaining why the bones of 1/7 are in 1/4, and the unfinished business here relates to that, not to the process of the entire autopsy, you know, and you're now taking it from here to something else. It's unfinished business in the sense that if you end up with 1/7 and 1/7A only, you haven't found the other body part. Therefore, when you go to 1/4 and you find that, in fact, the unfinished business gets finished in 1/4. That's where you find the body part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with the process of autopsy-taking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay, I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, do you have any knowledge of what happens to the samples once they're taken away from you by ICMP and they conduct their analysis? Do you have any role in that process?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is a question that has been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm unaware of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead and ask your question and [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Doctor, if I could put the question to you again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of what happens to -- what procedure is carried out once ICMP take the sample from you and conduct their DNA analysis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: The information that I was supposed to have in that sense was how to take a sample, how to transport it, and how to hand it over to the ICMP. Once the sample enters their laboratory, it's their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, this Trial Chamber has heard from a witness who explained that the DNA report that we have on the screen in front of us does not provide official confirmation that body remains have been identified, and that witness explained that in order to obtain official verification, you would need to look at the identification records. Would you agree with that witness's comment? Perhaps I can just explain. What he said about these reports is the one that we're looking at --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay, is he quoting now, Your Honour? If he's quoting, that's one thing, but I don't want him to paraphrase what the witness -- previous witness had said. I object if he's going to paraphrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to put the quotation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Say that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I was going to put the quotation to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe put the quotation to the witness before you solicit an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: What the witness stated, Doctor, is -- in relation to these DNA reports: "The one that we are looking at is just the working document, so to speak." That is what the witness said about these DNA reports, and he explained that in order to obtain official verification of body remains, he would need to look at the identification records. Would you agree with that witness's comment?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, you've put that a little strangely, but I think I understand what you mean. This finding does not mean that the identification has been complete, completed. Is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: So once I received this finding, it's definitive as far as the profession goes, professionalism and so on, because it's confirmation of identity. However, it's just one component, because when I receive a finding like this, when I've got these findings, then the family comes in, and every time, if we have arrived at an identity on the basis of this document, at least that's how I work it, the family takes another look at the body, and if there are any specific features, whether it's an old fracture or a jutting jaw, so that the antemortem and the postmortem match. And sometimes when you're doing that, despite the findings, despite what you found on the body, the family might not accept the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And did that happen in this case, do you know? Did the family -- did that further stage take place?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: I never came into contact with the families. I never met them myself, nor did I do anything with respect to identification, except for these findings, and sent this on to the Republika Srpska Commission. And, actually, I don't think they send the findings to me anymore, because I haven't received any for a long time now. So I think they keep them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question, Doctor. This procedure takes place afterwards, and this would have continued in Banja Luka, given that the bodies were sent there. The bodies were sent to Banja Luka after this first stage in the procedure; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could be. Where the bodies are located, that's where the identification takes place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And is it right that after the final stage takes place and the parties are satisfied that there has been a proper verification of a body, that an identification record is completed? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: When I identify bodies in my line of work, when the family accepts the body, then the minutes or a record is kept about the identification, and the signatories to that are the family members, on the one side, and on the other you have the doctor, the cantonal prosecutor, and a representative of the Federal Commission for Missing Persons, and a MUP inspector.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And they would all actually sign that document?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we look at the DNA reports in front of us, we can see one signature in the bottom left-hand corner. Do you know whose signature that is?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: You mean on the right-hand side or the left?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Right-hand.

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there's just one signature on the right, and that's an ICMP employee.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And does that signature indicate anything to you?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: It should indicate that they confirm that these causes -- rather, that these samples belong to that person, just the way in which I signed my finding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We can see that there's no signature from any -- or as far as I can see, there's no signature on this document from any forensic officer or doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But, Mr. Robson, this witness is an expert. She's really coming to opine on the autopsy. This thing comes from the ICMP, where she doesn't work. How is she to explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat what she said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can explain this. It's not a record on identification; it's the findings of the laboratory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's true, but the purpose for which you have been called here to come and testify goes beyond this question, even if you can answer it. You may answer if you want to, but I'm just trying to remind counsel your status and what may and may not be asked to you. But counsel for the Prosecution was on her feet, too. Did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I wasn't getting the interpretation, but I am now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may answer, now that you say you want to answer, ma'am. But please bear that in mind, Mr. Robson, with subsequent questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not the record of the identification where we all sign, it's just the findings from the laboratory. Just when you have surgical findings, the surgeon just signs, not the family and the patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robson. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Just a couple, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: While we're on the subject of identification, Doctor, my -- I get the sense there are two -- the word "identification" is being used in different ways in terms of your testimony. Do you have any reason to doubt that the DNA reports -- the accuracy of the DNA reports where they identify the owner of the particular bones from which the DNA samples were taken?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: The DNA findings are the ultimate, end findings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you talk about the -- all the remaining tasks that have to do with identification, are you referring to what the formal steps are that are taken with regard to the federation commission, when they come to the conclusion with regard to identification of bodies; is that what you are talking about here today?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: What I'm talking about is the process for identification which we conduct after exhumation, and that's always a set procedure. When we receive the DNA analysis, which we consider to be a valid finding, since the family -- and they're mostly people who don't understand what DNA means at all and that you can identify someone on the basis of something taken from bones, they still look for something they can relate to on the bones, something familiar to them. And if you can find a detail which can confirm what they know or think they know, then, in human terms, it's more -- it's easier for them to accept identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. One other question. Can you tell us, with regard to the bodies 1/1 through 1/7, excuse me, whether any -- and I do believe you refer to this in your report, that some of the bodies were bound, their hands, their arms or legs were bound. Can you tell me how many of those bodies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this question does not touch upon any issues discussed during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour, because the cross-examination was -- seemed to be steering the witness -- or not "steering the witness," but presenting an issue where the bones were just thrown into a grave, and I think that the -- I want to re-query the witness on -- that's not exactly what it -- the picture should be, that there were some intact, major portions of the body. And that's clear from her report, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then why do you want to rehash it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Because I want to give the witness the opportunity to explain it clearly on the record rather than just submit the report. I mean, I just think it -- it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Sartorio, the issue you are raising seems to be one of the time that elapsed between the first burial and the removal, because what you're implying is that if the bodies were removed while they were still held together by skin and tissue, then they would be found in the second grave, the skeleton would be found in the second grave in good order, so to say, where the right bones would lie next to the right bones. If, however, the body had become a skeleton before it was removed the second time, then the bones would have been found in disorder. That's the implication. But why is this relevant?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It's -- well, I would argue that it's not relevant whether there was a secondary grave, but I think that the Defence has raised it, and I feel the need to address it. Okay, I have no further questions, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a few question from me, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: With respect to skeleton 1/7, you say that that skeleton, in your report, still had a head. Do I read your report correctly?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that one body was a body with a head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And yet you attribute death to severance of the head? Do I still read your report correctly there?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you have understood what body we're dealing with and what the cause of death was. But since in this report you have a section where it says that the lower part of the body -- of the third cervical vertebra was of a smooth cut surface, that's why I'm saying this. When it says "severance of the body from the head," I said that because of the changes found on the vertebrae, when I stated my views on the probable cause of death, not only because the skull was in a different place to the body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me try and find out if I understand you clearly. The body -- the head was still attached to the body, but just the vertebra was severed; is that what you are saying or am I misunderstanding you?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: The head was in continuity of the body. You have the body, and it continues on to the head. In between were these changes on the vertebrae that we found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That clears me there. Then with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on a second. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I thought you also said that the head had been found in a different place in the grave, in a plastic bag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not 1/ 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Still staying with the body of number 7, are you able to explain the dental status that you mention there? You have mentioned figures there, teeth missing during life, 36, 46; teeth missing after death, 11, 12, 21, 35, 37, 42." What do these figures mean?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: When you look at the tooth status according to the chart you have, then these are teeth in the upper jaw. They range from 1 to 18 on the right side, and on the left side from 21 to 28. If you look at the lower jaw, they range from 31 to 38, because you have eight teeth to half a jaw, and then from 41 to 48 on the other side of the lower jaw, of course. Now, on the skeleton you can differentiate whether a tooth went missing during the person's lifetime, while he was still alive, so the person was missing that tooth from before. On the basis of what the tooth ridges looked like, if you look at the tooth ridges --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But what I'm trying to find out by these numbers, do these numbers represent the number of teeth? What do they represent?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: The number of the tooth. Eleven is the first sequitur on the right-hand side in the upper jaw, so the tooth number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me tell you why I'm asking the question so that you can clear me. My primary school education told me that an adult person has 32 teeth, and now these numbers, they go beyond 32. You know, you've got a 36, 46, 37, 42. That's what confuses me, and that is why I'm asking you what these numbers represent.

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: If you add them up, from 1 to 18 is eight [as interpreted]. From 27 to 28 [as interpreted] is eight. Sixteen, upper jaw. And from 31 to 38, eight, from 41 to 48, eight, so eight plus eight's 16 for the lower jaw. So 16 on top, 16 on the bottom jaw makes 32. You were taught correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hope somebody understands all this. I don't. I must be very slow on the uptake. But why do you use, what is that, 27 to 28, 1 to 18? What is this 1 to 18?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: I have an example of the diagram here. If I were to write the first sequitur or third pre-molar or fourth molar, then my findings would be over a large number of pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. My last question to you: Am I right to say during evidence-in-chief you explained the difference in the use within your report of the word "damage" and "injury"?

utterances.speaker: SABIHA SILAJDZIC-BRKIC
utterances.text: When I speak about damage, when I say "damage," the word itself says that something has been damaged, that there is damage, whether through the effects of climatic elements, or the place, the location, so through unintentional acts you get damage. When I say "injuries" or "wounds," "injuries," then injuries are injuries, whether you inflict them upon yourself or they are inflicted upon you by others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor. I just wanted to make sure that I understood you clearly on that last point. That's all I wanted to ask. Any questions arising, Madam Sartorio?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't even want to clear up 1 to 18 and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Doctor, thank you so much. This brings us to the conclusion of your testimony for now. Let me remind -- I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We'll be filing a motion tomorrow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you will discuss that with the witness, I don't have to mention it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I can't talk to her if she's coming back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Do I then have to remind her?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I would appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Doctor, you realise that you were not asked questions about teeth and about -- except for what I've just asked you, and about the eighth body. That is because that part of your report has not been -- has only just been found, and not everybody had seen it. So you probably will be approached to come back, to come and testify on that part sometime. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And the skulls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, I beg your pardon, and, yes, that's why I said the teeth. The skulls, actually, the skulls. So you will be called to come back to testify on those. Unfortunately, it happened that way. We didn't want it to happen that way, and I know it disturbs you in your own busy schedule, but please, I hope you understand. Okay? So for now, this brings us to the conclusion of your testimony. You are excused. You may go back home now, and please travel safely, but do expect that you may be called or will be called again. Okay? Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. That brings us to the end of the day. We're sitting tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning in Courtroom I. Okay, Courtroom I tomorrow morning. Court adjourned.
